pages.text:
*Ama's Stall Ledger, Night 61. Bowls sold: 0 (rain). Umbrellas borrowed: 63. Lanterns saved: all but one.*

The rain did not arrive. It crashed. By four o'clock, the gutters were running brown with silt and the sound was a solid wall of noise that swallowed every other sound in the lane. I stood in the middle of the wet asphalt, holding Jun's half-melted rooster lantern. The paper was soft and heavy in my hands, the red paint running down the wire frame in long, ugly streaks. It looked less like a bird and more like a sad, wet leaf caught in a drain.

Around me, the strings of lanterns sagged. The rain hammered against the paper, turning the bright colors into muddy smears. I took a step forward, then back. The water in my boots was cold and deep. I looked up at the dark sky, waiting for it to stop, but the clouds only grew heavier. The air smelled of wet dust and fear. I was alone with a melting bird and a sky that did not care.
pages.image: A small girl in a green padded jacket stands in the center of a wet night market lane, holding a dripping, melting red paper lantern, with heavy rain falling around her and dark wet ground.

pages.text:
Ama did not shout. She did not panic. She simply walked to the edge of her stall and began pulling the heavy canvas tarp down over the tables. Her movements were quick and sure, despite the rain soaking through her floral vest. Then she turned to the sky, looked at the hanging lanterns, and started climbing the small ladder by the pot.

Uncle Feng saw her. He bellowed for ladders, his voice cutting through the rain like a knife. Auntie Ping was already on her phone, talking fast, coordinating umbrellas from every stall. Jun, Yi-Chen, and Hui-Ting ran out from the arcade, splashing into the lane. We formed a line. Jun held the first lantern, passing it to Yi-Chen, who passed it to Hui-Ting, who passed it to me. It was a chain of hands in the rain, moving fast, keeping the light dry.
pages.image: A line of people in raincoats and aprons pass a glowing paper lantern along a chain of hands in a rainy night market, Lin, an eleven-year-old girl with a chin-length black bob and straight bangs, in a dark green padded jacket and a red-and-white checked apron, among them, while Ama in her flowery vest climbs a small ladder in the background. All shop signs, banners and hanging boards are smooth plain solid-color cloth.

pages.text:
For three hours, the lane turned into a wet, muddy river of people. Shop owners and school kids worked side by side, passing lanterns from hand to hand. Yi-Chen’s mother arrived in a clean coat, holding a tray of towels that looked like they had never seen dirt. Even Jun’s father came, still wearing his white Sky Mall apron. His face was serious. He was taking this very seriously.

Ama stood at the end of the line, near the temple. She wore her plastic sandals, and the rain swirled around her ankles. A bright yellow lantern was passed down to her. She held it gently, checking the wires with her damp hands. Then she looked at me. Across the rain. Across the wet lane.

She smiled. It was a small smile, but it was there.

I felt the knot in my chest loosen, just a little. She passed the lantern to the next person, and the line kept moving.
pages.image: Ama, a small grandmother in a flowery vest and plastic sandals, stands in the rain at the end of a line of people holding a glowing yellow lantern and smiling, while Lin, an eleven-year-old girl with a chin-length black bob and straight bangs, in a dark green padded jacket and a red-and-white checked apron, watches her from a few steps away.

pages.text:
By eight o'clock, the rain had thinned into a fine mist. The lane was quiet, except for the dripping water and the soft hum of the electric heaters. Sixty-three umbrellas were leaned against the temple wall, a colorful pile of red and blue and yellow plastic.

We gathered in the dry space of Mr. Tsai’s shop. The air smelled of old wood and dried spices. Jun held up his rooster lantern. It had melted into a mild abstract shape, the red and yellow mixed into a single, blurry blob. He looked at it, then at the group.

"It looks better this way," he said, shrugging.

Nobody argued. Hui-Ting nodded. Yi-Chen laughed. I picked up my own lantern, which had come through the storm intact, and held it next to Jun's. It was strange, and it was perfect.
pages.image: A group of young people standing in a shop with wooden shelves, holding up a melting, abstract red and yellow paper lantern, smiling at each other in warm light.

pages.text:
I went home with wet hair plastered to my forehead and a drip running down the back of my neck. The apartment was warm, but I could not sleep. I lay on the balcony, looking out at the dark lane. The air smelled of wet stone and star anise.

I held the old brass ladle. It was dented and heavy, Ama’s mother’s ladle. I had been afraid today, but the fear was gone. Tomorrow, the stranger would come. I would serve two bowls of soup. One would be Ama’s, the classic, the river that had flowed for forty years. The other would be mine, the one I had learned to make. Both were real. Both were mine. I closed my eyes and listened to the last drops of rain hitting the pavement.
pages.image: Lin, an eleven-year-old girl with a chin-length black bob and straight bangs, in a dark green padded jacket, lies on a small balcony at night holding an old dented brass ladle, looking out at a dark quiet lane with wet pavement reflecting faint light. All shop signs, banners and hanging boards are smooth plain solid-color cloth.
